utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Having heard all the caveats this morning, may I ask the Defence now to introduce its case. Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I have written my opening statement in B/C/S. So I hope you don't mind. I'm too tired to translate it now simultaneously, so I would prefer to have my opening statement in B/C/S, with your permission, Your Honours. Thanks. [Interpretation] To begin with, I should like to thank you on behalf of the accused, Dr. Stakic, for allowing us to address you in our brief before we start our case. Dr. Stakic's Defence is confident that it will prove during its case that eight counts of the fourth amended indictment need to be rejected. At the end of the case, Dr. Stakic will be acquitted. The Defence will refute and prove that the charges brought against Dr. Stakic are not true and that they are far from the standard which the Prosecution needs to meet; that is, to prove the guilt of the accused beyond any reasonable doubt. The Defence expects to prove that the evidence produced by the Prosecution is inconsistent, inaccurate, taken out of the context, and inadmissible. When the Prosecution's evidence is compared with the Defence's evidence, and expected testimonies of our witnesses, it will become obvious that this evidence offers -- I mean the evidence of the Prosecution is not reliable, and it all has to do with the onus probandi, with the burden of proof. And it will also be obvious that the Prosecution's evidence cannot show any involvement of Dr. Stakic in the activities described in the fourth amended indictment. In the course of its case, the Defence will prove that what is claimed by the Prosecution is not only inaccurate, but that it is above all impossible. The Defence case has been presented in our brief, and in it can be found the basis underpinning our Defence. I will now merely briefly go through certain things which are not covered by the brief. When we consider the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and when we think about it, we must be aware that this conflict broke out on the basis of two concepts. One was for the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia, and the other concept was for the continued stay of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Yugoslavia. The former concept, that is, the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was by and large the option of two peoples, the Croat and the Muslim peoples. The Muslim people later on was renamed as the Bosniak people. And the continuing stay of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Yugoslavia was by and large the option of the Serb people. The reason for the secession was not the inadequacy of rights enjoyed by the peoples who were for the secession because all the peoples both formerly and de facto in the Former Yugoslavia enjoyed the same rights. Why, then, did the Muslims want to secede? They wanted it because shortly after the secession, in view of their high birthrate, they would have become an absolute majority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if the principle of one man, one vote were applied, they would then in no time at all become the only rulers, the only governors, of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why did the Croats want the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina? The Croats wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to secede so that it could -- that they could easier detach the Croat parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Bosnia-Herzegovina and annex them to Croatia. Although in the beginning, both the Croat and the Muslim people wanted the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina because of the different concepts. The war between them in Bosnia-Herzegovina also broke out shortly afterwards. The Muslims were represented on rump bodies of the former Socialist Republic of the Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in these rump authorities of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were no representatives of the Serb and the Croat peoples elected by voters. In these authorities, in these agencies, there were some representatives of the Serb and the Croat peoples who the Muslim authorities have brought into these institutions to serve as ornaments. So even when we see a Croat or a Serb represented on a Muslim agency or a body, we can still be certain that in no way either in terms of their number or in terms of the -- of their weight could they participate or have a say or influence the -- any decisions taken by those agencies. The Croats were embodied and represented through the Croat Defence council, the HVO, which is the military force of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and through political, that is, legislative, and executive bodies of Herceg Bosna, and the judicial bodies of Herceg Bosna. So when we speak about the bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the Bosniak side never tires of insisting and the OTP as well, there were no such bodies. That is, it was not only the Serbs who set up political bodies separated from the rump bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the same was done by the Croats. We have three peoples with three separate political systems in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time under our consideration. Who starts the conflict? The Office of the Prosecutor alleges that the conflict is started by the one who wants the status quo. The Serbs want the status quo. The Serbs want Yugoslavia to survive. Who wants changes? Croats and Muslims want changes. They aspire to secession. It is theirs to set the action into motion. In our case, we shall show that both factually and from the point of politics and from a point of law, the Serbs are merely reacting to the actions of the other side. In Prijedor, the situation may not be viewed in isolation from all the other developments in the Balkan peninsula as of 1990. We must realise that there was a war in Croatia; we must realise that before the war in Croatia, there was a war in Slovenia. We must realise that as early as 1990, the constitution of Croatia turned the Serb people into a national minority. And it was this already which caused numerous refugees from Croatia who headed towards Bosnia and Serbia. And especially and in particular, the beginning of the war set in motion huge numbers of people from Croatia heading for Bosnia and Serbia. All this must be borne in mind if one is to understand how the political life in the municipality of Prijedor unfolded. On the 30th of April, 1992, the Serbs take over the power. We see that there are no reprisals after that date. However even before the takeover of power, and especially after it, the Bosniak/Croat armed forces across Bosnia and Herzegovina launch armed operations against the JNA and against the armed forces of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its civilian population. There are also orders of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina going in on which the Serb people is not represented go in the same direction. There is also the order of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina going in the same direction. His name is Alija Delimustafic, and he also orders attacks on columns, military facilities, because under a pretext that allegedly the property of Bosnia and Herzegovina is being misappropriated. Some of these attacks -- these attacks include the attacks on Hambarine on the 22nd of May, 1992; the attack on the army column in Jakupovici in the area of Kozarac on the 24th of May, 1992; attack on the town of Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992. In response to these attacks, the armed forces of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, subsequently Republika Srpska, use force. We shall prove during our case that not only as the Prosecution claims the Crisis Staff was not -- did not make part of the chain of command in the military units, but moreover, that it had no, and we emphasise absolutely no, say or any knowledge about the activities, about the actions, of the army unless the army was ready and willing to inform them about. The Crisis Staff could not even request to be informed, not only -- they could not order, they could not even ask the military what they were doing. And the same, absolutely the same, holds true of the police which is also an armed force of the republic -- of Republika Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srpska. The attacks on military facilities and columns in the spring of 1992 came from the central offices of the Party for Democratic Action headed by Alija Izetbegovic. At that time, the presidency, the rump presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dissolved the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina from which the representatives of the Serb people were already absent, and unlawfully and unconstitutionally takes over the functions of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is, they won't even bother to request that the representatives of the Croat and Bosniak peoples vote for something that they need; they simply take everything into their own hands. And even that was not enough. Alija Izetbegovic unlawfully and unconstitutionally proclaims himself the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although such an office is not envisaged either by the constitution or by the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And finally, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, after all the political struggles and attempts to avoid violent secession begins a few days after the unlawful referendum. The referendum is unlawful not only because the representatives of the Serb people did not participate in its organisation, but also because its result which is below 66.6 per cent, the first findings say that 57 per cent turned out at the referendum. Later on, however, these results were changed to reach 64 per cent. And even that was not enough. Even if one takes that everybody went out, that it was 100 per cent turnout, and that they all voted for, even that is not enough for any changes of the constitution or any secession. A few days after the referendum, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started. And the witnesses who have come to testify this week will testify about that. So these are not witnesses who are to testify on the basis of tu quoque. [In English] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Can we make a short break. Dr. Stakic has to go out for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes to 12.00. --- Break taken at 11.43 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We apologise for this interruption, Your Honours, and thank you. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the incursion of the regular Croatian forces into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina occurred on the 3rd of May, 1992. After that, on the 26th of March, there was the massacre of Serb civilians in the village of Sijekovac in Bosanski Brod Municipality which was also covered in all the media, and members of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the scene. Only several days later, Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by the European Community, even though at that time there were still calls for caution that such recognition might lead to dreadful consequences and to an all-out war across Bosnia and Herzegovina. This may be pleasant or less pleasant for someone to hear, but it is a fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina was shattered and pushed into war as well as the whole of the Former Yugoslavia by the so-called international community. When I say "international community," it is clear that I am speaking about all the leading countries of the western hemisphere. The people who resisted this attempt to shatter their state was marked off as the guilty party and the party to blame for everything which later occurred in the framework of the conflict in the Former Yugoslavia. The other two peoples who took part in this breakup, who cooperated in the breakup of the Former Yugoslavia, were spared such attacks and spared the sanctions later imposed by the same international community. Who did the western countries, above all, the NATO countries, side with? They clearly displayed their allegiances when in the middle of peace negotiations, they blamed the Serb side in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina equally. Of course, this eventually led to the bombing, the bombing attacks, against the federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1999 by the NATO forces. In order to divert attention from this plan to shatter Yugoslavia, a joint criminal enterprise allegedly perpetrated by the Serbs is invented. What sort of a plan should the Serbs have had to remain in a state in which they already were? All Serbs lived within a single state. This theory cannot be confirmed by any means. If we know that the Serbs had no need to do anything, take any action whatsoever in order to achieve what they wanted, they wanted Yugoslavia. They wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of that state. They have the Yugoslavia they want. They have Bosnia within Yugoslavia. Why would they need to do anything at all? The next theory used against the Serbian people is the alleged theory of the attempt to create Greater Serbia. This was a theory employed a long time ago by the Austro-Hungarian monarchy when it annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina within its own borders. This theory was revived in World War I. And then again in the 1990s. Such a plan was never part of Serbian or Yugoslav policy. There is no trace that there ever was such a plan as part of a Serbian policy. We shall put forward this theory using a book written by a Muslim general, this theory that Yugoslavia was shattered by the leading western forces. This is the plan which caused Yugoslavia to break up. The entire situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina led to a state of insecurity and fear. No one knew to what extent conflicts would escalate, how long they would last, or which areas would be encompassed by the war. As we've said before, it began in Slovenia, continued in Croatia, and then spread to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The whole territory of the Former Yugoslavia was being abandoned by a great number of people, and the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, too, was being abandoned by people en masse, prior to the 30th of April, 1992. Same goes for Prijedor municipality, many people were leaving prior to the 30th of April, 1992. And all Prosecution witnesses who claimed that they had no knowledge of people leaving before the takeover, they all lied. It was not possible not to know, not to notice, large groups of people appearing daily at the Prijedor bus terminal waiting for buses to leave Prijedor through Croatia for third countries in western Europe or to stay in either Croatia or Slovenia and find refuge there. We shall show written proof of this, and we expect our witnesses to tell you exactly how many people had left before the takeover, how many people had left Prijedor Municipality. It is our submission, and we expect to be able to prove this, that prior to the 30th of April, 1992, more than 20.000 Muslims and Croats left Prijedor Municipality. Some Serbs left, too. However, their departure was not as conspicuous, because there were many refugees coming in, Serb refugees from Croatia. 200.000 refugees from Croatia passed through Prijedor during the conflict. Even as we speak, there are still 37.000 of those refugees living in Prijedor. In 1990, political parties who took power at the elections in November 1990, SDA, SDS, and HDZ, all had the preservation of Yugoslavia as an important feature of their programmes. In 1991, there were international conferences. The first one was in The Hague. And several of the later ones were held in The Hague also. There was the Lisbon conference, the London conference, negotiations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. All the conclusions from those conferences point to the fact that Yugoslavia should remain as it was, so the claims made by the Prosecution in the fourth amended indictment can by no means be confirmed; namely, that it was obvious that Croatia would secede, that it was obvious that SDS would not be able to prevent Bosnia and Herzegovina from seceding. The SDS did not need to do anything to prevent secession because the only secession there could have been would have been an unconstitutional and unlawful one. And this political action saw the SDS and the SDA join forces just after their election victory with the SDS and after they joined a coalition in 1992. Correction, the HDZ and the SDA took this political action. And in 1992, they formed a coalition with the SDS in order to take power. In the course of our case, we shall prove that only several months after the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. election victory of November 1990, the HDZ and the SDA began to prepare the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia. This is not only being done politically, but also by creating each their own armed forces. Throughout this time, the SDS did not work towards creating their own armed forces. The SDS believed that the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, was the only legal armed force in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When you look at the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, at that time, it was fully isolated in terms of its territory from all other Serb territories and encircled by the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, the HDZ, and the SDA in Bosnia. In addition to this threat of an armed attack, this isolation caused all goods to be in short supply. I'm talking about such goods as basic food stuffs, medicines, fuel, electricity, which in turn caused shortage of water, drinking water, created a situation where it was not possible to administer surgical treatment and so on and so forth. This all very much affected not only the lives of people in the town of Prijedor, but also of those who were captured and held detained in investigation centres. Again, we would like to point out that in our case, we shall prove that Dr. Milomir Stakic was never present in any of these collection or investigative centres and was in no way associated with these investigation centres. At the time the conflict broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, mainly the laws of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia were still valid, as well as the laws of the Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So these laws applied also to the territory of Vitez municipality as well as Konjic municipality. Presidents of the Vitez and Konjic municipalities were never convicted by this Tribunal, and there were camps in their territory, too. And Ivica Santic indeed was tried before this Tribunal, but the Prosecution gave it up. The president of the Municipal Assembly of Konjic and the Konjic war presidency testified before this Tribunal, but he was never indicted. So much for de jure responsibility of Dr. Stakic. In our case, we shall prove that the social federative Republic of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were both part of a legal system in which even the smallest thing, even the smallest legal area, even the smallest area of everyday life was strictly regulated through laws and bylaws. In the Former Yugoslavia, there were over 7 million different kinds of laws. That was a consequence of socialist self-management. Everything was prescribed by laws and bylaws. Nothing could be done unless it had first been prescribed by a law. It would not have been possible for the president of the Municipal Assembly to give orders to the army, to command the army or to command the police. It would have been inconceivable for the president of the Municipal Assembly to even command the firemen in Prijedor Municipality. The president of the Municipal Assembly and the position of the Municipal Assembly was later taken over by the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality, the president could only do exactly what they read out to us from the statute of the Municipal Assembly by the witnesses of the Prosecution. He could only preside over the meetings of the Municipal Assembly, and in cooperation with the president of the Executive Board, he could set the agenda for the Assembly's work. And then even that agenda had to be approved by and passed by the Municipal Assembly. I know that this may be confusing for people who come from the west who have mayors in their own legal systems. These two positions have nothing at all in common. Nothing at all. Nowadays in the legal system of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you have the head or the mayor of the Municipal Assembly. And you have the president of the Municipal Assembly. The president of the Municipal Assembly had no power to do anything that was not regulated by positive laws and bylaws or prescribed as part of his duty and area of competence. The same applies to the president of the Crisis Staff. The Prosecution knows this full well. That's why they gave up prosecuting Ivica Santic. As far as the factual power and role of the 29-year-old completely anonymous in the town of Prijedor Dr. Milomir Stakic is concerned, we should try to show in the course of our case what influence exactly he held, that is how powerless he was. As concerns Dr. Stakic, as the president of the council for National Defence of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, we shall prove that the last time this council met was on the 15th of May, 1992. Even that body had no power to order anything. That body could not even request information from the army or the police, for that matter. After the 15th of May, 1992, that body only met again in September, in late September, I think, of 1992. We shall prove that the army and the police have their own chains of command and that as such, they are absolutely and fully independent, independent from any municipal organ. In our case, we shall prove what the main reason was that the Bosniak/Muslim people started leaving the territory of Prijedor Municipality. We shall prove that all military-aged men were liable for military service. Even Serbs who failed to respond to the callups were persecuted, tried, and convicted. And we shall present the Court with documents in writing testifying to this effect. That was the main idea of male Bosniaks and Croats, driving them to leave the territory of Republika Srpska. They did not wish to serve in the Republika Srpska army. As for Dr. Stakic's responsibility, the Defence will mainly be divided up into a number of levels. First we shall call witnesses of different nationalities. We hope that Muslim, Serb, Croat, and Ukrainian witnesses will appear before this Court because all these different ethnic groups are represented in Prijedor Municipality. I think we even have a Polish witness. The Defence will try to call witnesses who were captured in Prijedor and outside Prijedor, and those witnesses will testify as to who was in command and what exactly Dr. Stakic's role was in 1992. We shall show by using independent documents and witnesses that Dr. Stakic had no genocidal intent or the mens rea necessary for the commission of any crime as charged in the fourth amended indictment. We shall use documents and witness testimonies to prove that Dr. Stakic had no knowledge of criminal activities taking place during that period in Prijedor Municipality. Yes indeed, at a later stage, he was in a position to learn about some of them, just like most inhabitants of Prijedor did learn about these things, but only after a period of time had elapsed. Expert and factual witnesses will be called to deny the theories presented by the Prosecution against Dr. Stakic and connected to the relationship between Dr. Stakic and the army and Dr. Stakic and the police. The relationship between the local politicians, the politicians, and Dr. Stakic. We also wish to deny the Prosecution claims concerning the demographic makeup of the population throughout the war and after the war. Our intention was also to call a forensic witness, a forensic expert, especially in the light of testimonies by witnesses that we spoke about just this morning where a witness claims that after a brief while, Dr. Stakic did not even attend the meetings of the Crisis Staff any more. Would that expert witness give a different testimony if he had known about this? At this moment, do we really need to have this testimony, this expert testimony, where the witness will be able to tell us that Dr. Stakic did not even attend the meetings of the Crisis Staff at that moment? And it is our submission that he didn't even sign those documents because those documents contain as many as six different signatures. And this was established also through the testimony of the expert witness of a graphologist during the Prosecution's case. We also wanted to call a media analyst who would analyse the disgraceful, the shameful testimony of the journalist Vulliamy. And we do not know whether the prosecutors' Office is ready to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Defence counsel to calm down and to use the appropriate words in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Office of the Prosecutor realises that this witness in at least two different cases testified in two completely different ways with regard to the same facts. And we shall Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. request that the OTP bring charges against that witness, and that is why we want to bring in a media analyst to testify in our case. Likewise, an historian is coming to refute the Prosecution's allegations regarding the historical backdrop of the conflict. A constitutional law expert has been envisaged to come and show how laws in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina and the municipality of Prijedor worked which were the real terms of reference of Dr. Stakic's. We think it is better to prove that through expert witnesses than through car mechanics, truck drivers, and electrical engineers. If we want to know how law functioned we are not ready before this Chamber to prove legal aspects through car mechanics. Why didn't the OTP call any expert on constitutional law or local self-government? Because such an expert cannot say what they need to hear. Next -- after them, we should have witnesses who are friends, neighbours, and relatives of Dr. Stakic. And they are to tell the Court what was Dr. Stakic like before the conflict, during the conflict, and after the conflict and all that happened in 1992. They will be coming here to testify about their relations with Dr. Stakic before April 1992, in April 1992, his attitude to propaganda, broadcasts on television or radio, and press statements. They are also to show what was the relationship of Dr. Stakic with other nongovernmental organisations, his attitude towards Muslims and Croats. The standing of Dr. Stakic in the neighbourhood community he lived in. These witnesses will prove that Dr. Stakic never visited Omarska, never saw Keraterm, never went to Trnopolje. The only thing that the Office of the Prosecutor has succeeded in bringing before this Chamber is a witness with very poor eyesight, and the Defence has come by evidence to show that that witness was suffering from mental traumas; that is, that that person suffered from mental disorders before the war. We also saw what poor eyesight that man suffered from, and he admitted before this Chamber that he did not have the eyeglasses in Omarska and yet he claimed to have recognised Dr. Stakic from a distance of 70 metres. And finally, the Defence believes that the documentation that was disclosed to it under Rule 68, that is, the part that was disclosed to us, that was given us, even though it is evident that the large part of this documentation has never been turned over to the Defence and the witness statements will suffice to refute the Prosecution's allegations as stated in the fourth amended indictment. And in themselves, they constitute more than a sufficient reason to acquit Dr. Stakic. It is the Defence's belief that on behalf of Dr. Stakic, that the evidence that we expect to produce will show and confirm the only logical truthful and fair conclusion, that Dr. Stakic is innocent under all counts of the fourth amended indictment filed against him. And finally, the Defence believes that this Honourable Court will find that the witnesses called by the Prosecution contradicting one another, inconsistent, and untrustworthy, and that its judgement will be in favour of Dr. Stakic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Dr. Stakic, you are aware as it has been said in the beginning of this case that whenever it's appropriate, this Trial Chamber will allow on your request to give a statement. At this point in time, Rule 84 bis provides especially that after the opening statement of a party, you have the right, if you so wish, to give a statement under this rule. Do you want to give such a statement now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not ready at this moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just clarify that by a statement, Your Honour at this stage is talking about evidence on oath as opposed to the type of statement that Your Honour had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At this moment, I make as hopefully one can see from the transcript, Rule 84 bis statement of the accused after the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's necessary to have the break now. And then immediately after the break, we will start with the first Defence witness. Please let us limit ourselves to, if possible, 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before Your Honour rises, Mr. Lukic talked about protective measures. We don't know why again there's a request for protective measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness is called, may I just mention very quickly either now or the end of the session today, because I can't be here tomorrow, would Your Honour allow me to raise two or three matters, short matters of administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first is this: Would Your Honour make an order that the transcripts of the summoned interviews which we are about to disclose in full should not be disseminated beyond the Defence team in this case. In other words, Your Honour, they should not be handed over to people not directly connected with the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We issue in -- issued in the beginning a general --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that applied to statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- that transcripts should be in an area of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's witnesses the Prosecution were intending to call. That's what the order deals with. These were not witnesses the Prosecution intends to call. So if Your Honour would be kind enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this is ordered as requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The second matter is this: Would Your Honour also be ordered that today we be supplied with proper summaries of the witnesses the Defence intend to call in the next -- in this week, plus the order of witnesses, plus proper details of the witnesses. Your Honour, and may I on that note just deal with this: That I understand why Your Honour has allowed this witness who is here to be called. But Your Honour one of the ways of dealing with this is that if witnesses have not yet been brought to this Tribunal and the evidence is as we anticipate it will be, all about the events in Bosanski Brod, which we're not going to dispute, that the other witnesses need not be called. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It is considerably expensive to the Tribunal to bring witnesses and the time taken up who are not actually strictly necessary to the issues in the case. But Your Honour I just mention that at this stage, but my concern is we get proper summaries as required under the rules and proper details and the order of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt, it's deplorable that we didn't receive this until today. But my assumption is that we will -- we have to stay realistic that we receive by the end of the day the order of the witnesses to be called tomorrow and the necessary summary. And as regards the other witnesses to appear during this week, no later by the end of tomorrow. But in general, we have to come back to these issues when discussing the 65 ter (g) motion as such. I think now we shouldn't hesitate any longer. And I would ask the usher to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, before the witness comes, Your Honour, I got one hour for the direct examination of this witness. Is it possible if we continue until 2.00? Because there is no other trial today in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We try our very best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the translation unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, my apologies that we address you only as Witness DA, which is a pseudonym. It's on the request of one of the parties for your protection. It's nothing with impoliteness, only for your own protection. So may we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. DA. We speak the same language, and in view of the interpretation, will you please wait a little before you answer my question so that the interpreters' service could interpret. For the record, will you tell us when were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I was born on the 15th of April, 1935 in Bosanski Brod, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I am married, but I do not know whether I'm still married. I am married, but I don't know if something has happened to that marriage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the ethnicity of your wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: She is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that you do not know whether you are still married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, I haven't for the past ten years -- divorced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it because your wife is afraid of the consequences if she came to live with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the reason something that you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if she came to live with you, would there be a risk of her losing her pension?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: She could lose both her pension and her relatives might also renounce her, disown her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is also the risk that her son who works in Croatia might lose his job, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. And that is why the two of us are suffering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Three. Because I had two sons when I married her, and she had one daughter when she married me. And our children were quite small when we were married, and we have been married for over 20 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one daughter is married, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. One daughter got married before the war, and she married -- she lives in Croatia and she is married to a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us briefly what happened on the 3rd of March, 1992? What happened to you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: That day, before that day, let me tell you just one sentence. There was war psychosis which one could feel in Croatia so that that day --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are sorry. We cannot hear the witness at all. We cannot hear the witness. We are sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Something is wrong with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not hear anything. We are sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we ask the booth, can you hear the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness needs to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I shall repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can barely hear him now. Could you repeat the previous question we think the witness said. But we can barely hear him, so this is not working really, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's try in the meantime let the technicians work on this problem, that you not only can barely hear the witness but entirely. But could you please rephrase your last question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to you on the 3rd of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Now we do not hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Our apologies. We have to wait for the technician. May I take the liberty in the meantime, and my apologies to the witness, in order to proceed with the second question raised by the Office of the Prosecution, that we discuss these issues in office in the framework of a 65 ter (i) conference this afternoon, say, at 4.00. Would this be appropriate for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry, I can't be here. I have to leave today at half past 2.00, but Mr. Koumjian will be here and he can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We can be here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So 4.00 in my office, please, for a 65 ter (i) conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I should say with Your Honour's permission, Ms. Karper as usual will be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That goes without saying. Apparently, the problems are related to voice distortion. Therefore, in order to continue, if there is no objection, we go into closed session. This is feasible. I can't see any objections. So therefore, we proceed in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 1.44 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of November, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
